executive_summary: AUD/CAD is at 0.99123 (gated store, spotDate 2026-10-02, one session after the valuation date). A rising pair means the Australian dollar is strengthening against the Canadian dollar. The pair is down 0.20% over one month and up 0.74% over three months, 1.28% over six and 8.41% over twelve. It sits at the 90th percentile of its 52-week closing range, 150 pips below the 1.0008 closing high set on 22 September at parity. The main story is that the two central banks have moved apart and the market prices each of them the wrong way round. The RBA's unanimous hike to 4.60% on 29 September widened the policy gap to +235bp, yet only about 20% of a further hike is priced for 3 November. Canada's two-year, meanwhile, prices 112bp of Bank of Canada tightening that the Bank's own 1.95% core measure does not support. Two points neither dossier captures on its own: Canadian oil sells at a discount, leaving a realised barrel near USD 76.70 against a Brent headline near USD 100, and the core-inflation gap between the two economies is 165bp, wider than the headline gap. The settled verdict is Bullish tactically (conviction 3, score +0.3222) and Bullish strategically (conviction 2, score +0.2150). Three things argue for caution. The chart shows a clean rejection at parity on 22–23 September. The four-provider consensus sits just below spot. And a moderation in Australian price pressures was reported on 5 October, after pass 1 scored. So the levels below treat parity as resistance until a daily close clears 1.00137, and size the trade to be tested cheaply.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The bilateral policy differential is +235bp in AUD's favour on the gated payload, with the RBA Cash Rate Target at 4.60% as of 2026-10-01 against the Bank of Canada Overnight Rate Target at 2.25% as of 2026-09-28, and the gap widened 25bp on 29 September when the RBA hiked unanimously while the Bank of Canada had just held for a seventh consecutive meeting. The direction of travel is the point rather than the level: one central bank has an explicitly retained hiking option and the other sits at the bottom of its own 2.25-3.25% neutral band with an operational core measure, the trim-median average, at 1.95% and below target. The long end agrees but less emphatically, with the payload's monthly August 10-year observations at 5.015% for Australia and 3.675% for Canada, a +134bp term spread, and the dossiers' live late-September cross-sections at 5.38% and 3.96% giving +142bp. The pricing asymmetry is the tactical edge and it points the same way on both legs: only about 20% of a 3 November RBA hike is discounted, while the Canadian curve prices roughly 120bp of Bank of Canada tightening to about 3.45% by September 2027 with the Canadian two-year at 3.37%, fully 112bp above the policy rate. The one scheduled repricing event inside the tactical window is the Bank of Canada decision on 28 October, which the gated calendar marks as a projection round carrying the Monetary Policy Report, and it is the asymmetric one: a hold that softens the oil assumption bleeds premium out of the Canadian front end with nothing on the Australian side to offset it until 3 November. Transmission is direct, through the cross-currency rate differential and the 235bp of carry a long position accrues.

tactical.what_is_priced: The market prices the RBA as finished and the Bank of Canada as about to start, which is the mirror image of what each bank's own core inflation measure supports. We think the 235bp differential is more likely to hold or widen than to compress inside four weeks, and the 28 October Monetary Policy Report is where that is first tested.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to three months the question is not whether the differential is wide but whether it survives, and the asymmetry of the two reaction functions says it largely does. The Bank of Canada has 50bp of room before policy becomes restrictive and a credible case for using none of it, with core at 1.95%, unemployment at 6.4%, August employment down 41,700 and wage growth halved to 2.0%; the RBA has trimmed mean stuck at 3.6%, 60bp above the top of its band, and a Board that has already hiked four times in 2026. Three further scheduled decisions fall inside the strategic horizon and the gated calendar dates them precisely: RBA on 3 November, RBA on 8 December and Bank of Canada on 9 December. The convergence the market prices requires Canada to deliver roughly 50bp over that window against a reaction function whose own operational core is below target, so the realistic range for the differential is roughly 210bp to 235bp rather than the 185bp or narrower that current Canadian front-end pricing implies. Carry is genuinely harvestable at this width: 235bp against an estimated 6.472% three-month implied volatility gives a ratio of 0.363, far better than the 0.117 AUD earns against USD and better than CAD earns anywhere except against CHF. The limiting factor, and the reason confidence is 58 rather than higher, is that the Australian labour market is inviting a pivot the market will price before the RBA delivers it, and RBC's published view that the yield thrust behind AUD is sputtering because the RBA is likely done is the coherent version of the counter-case.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The inflation differential between the two economies is the widest and most policy-relevant in the G10 commodity bloc once each central bank's own preferred core measure is used rather than the headline. Australia's trimmed mean is 3.6% and has been stuck there for three consecutive months, 60bp above the top of the 2-3% band; Canada's trim-median average is 1.95%, below the 2% target, with the 3.0% headline an artefact of gasoline at plus 22.8% year on year and CPI ex-gasoline at 2.4%. That is a 165bp core gap pointing in AUD's direction, and it is the gap that determines which central bank can afford to look through what. Growth reinforces it: Australian GDP is 2.14% year on year against Canada's 1.13%, the second lowest in the benchmarking set, and Canadian Q4 growth is estimated by its own governor at below 1% if tariffs persist, which they have. Labour markets differ in level more than direction - Australian unemployment at 4.6% against Canadian 6.4% - but the Canadian deterioration is faster, with employment down 41,700 in August and permanent-employee wage growth halved to 2.0%. Both economies' most consequential prints land inside the tactical window and both skew the same way for the pair: Canadian CPI on 19 October, where the gasoline base effect mechanically decays, and Australian September-quarter CPI on 28 October, where the monthly indicator has already re-accelerated to 4.0%. Asymmetric sensitivity favours the Canadian prints, because Canadian data has 112bp of embedded hike premium to disappoint while Australian data has only about 20% of a November hike to confirm.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to three months both economies deteriorate, and the bilateral question is only which deteriorates faster relative to what its central bank will tolerate. Australia's own dossier turns strategically bearish on growth - NAB business conditions negative at -2 for the first time since September 2020, sales margins at -20, purchase costs rising 1.2% a quarter against final prices of 0.5% - and that is a real constraint on how long the RBA can tighten. But Canada's deterioration is both further advanced and more structural: unemployment already at 6.4%, benchmark house prices down 3.0% year on year, building permits down 17.3% month on month, and a tariff regime that escalated from duty to outright import ban on 29 September and taxes the goods balance directly. The decisive asymmetry is the inflation floor. Australia's trimmed mean at 3.6% gives the RBA no room to turn dovish quickly even as growth softens; Canada's trim-median at 1.95% gives the Bank of Canada every excuse to stay put while the gasoline base effect pulls headline toward 2.2-2.6%. So the stagflationary configuration in Australia and the disinflationary-contraction configuration in Canada resolve to the same pair direction through the rate channel, which is why this factor stays Bullish strategically at a reduced 52 rather than flipping. Confidence is modest because the two bearish growth stories are genuinely comparable in size and the margin between them is a judgement about relative tolerance, not a measured differential.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: AUD/CAD is a low-beta risk cross, not a risk proxy: both legs are commodity currencies and the net equity sensitivity is the difference between AUD's high G10 risk beta and CAD's weakest-in-the-bloc equity correlation of -0.2 to -0.3 against the S&P 500. That residual is genuinely positive - a risk-off shock hurts AUD more than CAD, and the Canadian dossier explicitly identifies CAD strengthening against AUD, NZD and NOK in risk-off episodes - but it is a second-order effect at a 0.09 weight. The current cross-asset configuration is benign in equities and fraying in credit: VIX at 16.07 on 28 September sits at the 28th percentile of its one-year range, the S&P 500 is up 14.02% over twelve months, while US high yield has widened 42bp over the month to 302bp and investment grade at 83bp sits at the 86th percentile of its one-year range even though it is historically tight. The month's actual shock was in rates, not equities, with the US 10-year up 51bp to 5.24% at the top of its one-year range - a configuration that hurts AUD more than CAD and argues against pressing a bullish pair view on this factor. The domestic equity read cuts the other way, with the S&P/TSX down 2.85% over the month on banking and mining losses while energy producers rose. Those forces offset, and Neutral is the honest output rather than a failure to choose.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Strategically the risk channel for this pair reduces to two binaries that cut across each other. A Hormuz settlement is risk-positive and China-growth-positive, which helps AUD, while simultaneously collapsing the energy premium, which hurts CAD through terms of trade but also removes the RBA's stated justification for further tightening - so the sign on the pair is genuinely ambiguous. An escalation reverses every term. The China channel is the one differentiator with a clean sign and it is currently weak: Q2 GDP of 4.3% was the slowest since end-2022 and one month of NBS manufacturing PMI at 50.1 is not a demand impulse, so the iron-ore transmission that would make this a cleanly risk-on cross is dormant. The December Central Economic Work Conference is the dated event that could change that, and it falls inside the strategic window. Against it, Canada's risk exposure is idiosyncratic rather than global - a US trade conflict rather than a global growth cycle - which further decouples the two legs' risk betas and reduces the factor's discriminating power. At a 0.05 weight, Neutral at 50 is the defensible reading and the factor is explicitly not doing any work in the score.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: Both legs carry speculative short bases of almost identical size, which is the specific configuration in which the pair signal is muted rather than amplified. The CFTC legacy non-commercial net is short 46,814 AUD contracts on the 22 September report, while leveraged funds are short 46,861 CAD contracts on the same date and the Canadian headline non-commercial net is -53.2k. Short base against short base nets to approximately nothing for the cross. The complication on the Australian leg is that the two CFTC report families disagree outright - leveraged funds are net LONG 58,726 AUD contracts against the legacy short - so the level of AUD exposure cannot be established, and a positioning factor whose level is unknown cannot carry a directional stance. Both markets de-grossed hard: Australian open interest fell 37.8% in one week to 306,488 and Canadian open interest fell 13.1% to 311,085, which removes the leverage that amplifies squeezes in either direction. What is identifiable and pair-specific is crowding in the trade itself: long AUD/CAD appears as a recommended relative-value expression in both dossiers, UBS has published a long with an explicit target, HSBC has flagged the cross as a bullish thematic, and Pepperstone describes AUD long positioning in general as increasingly crowded. A consensus long is not a reason to be short, but it is a reason not to count positioning as a tailwind.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to three months positioning stops being a signal on both legs for the same reason: neither is at an extreme. The Australian legacy short of 46,814 contracts is roughly 58% of the plus-or-minus 80,000-contract threshold that has historically preceded AUD reversals, and the Canadian short of 46,861 sits comfortably inside the CAD brief's own -80k significance level, some 33,000 contracts away. There is nothing to mean-revert from on either side. The durable structural flows run in opposite directions and are of different kinds: Australian superannuation hedging is mechanically AUD-positive, with nearly nine in ten surveyed funds intending to raise hedge ratios and none intending to cut FX exposure, while Canadian portfolio repatriation produced a C$30.63bn net sale of foreign securities in August after a C$35.43bn purchase the prior month - a one-month swing of C$66bn that is too volatile to extrapolate. Canadian Q4 producer hedging is a seasonal CAD-positive inside the window, though weakened by a falling crude strip. Bilateral direct flows are immaterial: IMF DOTS puts two-way goods trade at roughly $4.8bn a year, so there is no trade-settlement channel of any consequence. Neutral at 44 reflects a genuine absence of signal plus an unresolved data conflict on the Australian leg, not a balanced judgement.

Australia's dominant export price is soft - iron ore at USD 96.59 a tonne is down 7.14% over twelve months and the forward estimate on the same source is lower still - while its energy complex is booming, with Newcastle coal up 36.72% and copper up 35.84%, and the RBA commodity price index up 15.5% year on year. The framework's direction rules would make oil up bearish for AUD/CAD, since oil is a strong CAD positive and only a mild AUD negative, but the Canadian capture problem blunts roughly a quarter of that, and oil has in any case retraced from USD 114.89 on 22 September. Bilateral trade is immaterial as a channel: IMF DOTS shows Australia exporting $2.1bn to Canada against $2.7bn of imports for a net balance of -$0.6bn, trivial against either economy, so this pair trades third-party commodity exposure rather than any direct flow. strategic.bilateral_analysis: This is the clearest strategic argument against the pair and it carries the second-heaviest strategic weight. The external-balance differential is stark and runs the wrong way for a long: Australia's current account deficit widened to AUD 27.2bn, or 3.666% of GDP, with the goods and services balance itself in deficit at AUD 5.1bn and net foreign debt at AUD 1,486.0bn, while Canada swung to a C$8.8bn surplus in Q2, 1.03% of GDP, its first since 2022 and the largest since 2005, on record C$60.6bn energy exports. That is a 4.7 percentage-point-of-GDP gap in Canada's favour. Valuation compounds it rather than offsetting it: the BIS real effective exchange rate puts AUD at 116.11, the highest in the benchmarking set and up 9.97% over twelve months, against CAD at 96.29, the second cheapest and down 1.67 points - a roughly 20-point real gap, accumulated while Australia's principal export price fell 7.14% and Canada's balance of payments improved by C$17bn quarter on quarter. A currency cannot appreciate 10% in real terms against deteriorating terms of trade and a widening external deficit indefinitely while its counterpart cheapens into a record surplus. The genuine offsets, and the reason confidence is 60 rather than 70, are that Canada's surplus is a price effect already reversing - the July trade balance collapsed to C$0.77bn and the Reuters consensus puts 2026 WTI at USD 83.90, below spot - that the WCS discount caps Canadian capture structurally, and that Section 338 import bans tax exactly the goods balance that produced the surplus.

net_commodity_exposure.net_effect_calculation: Applying the framework direction rules: oil up gives ++CAD and +AUD, so the net sign on AUD/CAD is negative, exactly as the framework's own AUD/CAD worked example states - CAD benefits more. Iron ore up gives ++AUD and is mildly negative for an importer, so the net sign is positive. LNG and JKM up is negative for importers and sometimes positive for AUD, with no clean CAD transmission. This cycle the two dominant legs are moving in opposite directions: Brent is up roughly 50% over twelve months while iron ore is down 7.14%, which on the raw rules is bearish for the pair. Two adjustments reduce that. First, Canada realises only about 77% of the Brent headline because of the Brent-WTI spread of USD 11.05 and the WCS discount of USD 14.80, so roughly a quarter of the oil impulse does not reach Canadian export revenue or the Canadian dollar. Second, Australia's non-iron-ore complex is doing unusual work, with coal up 36.72%, copper up 35.84% and the RBA commodity price index up 15.5% y/y, so the Australian terms-of-trade impulse is less negative than the iron-ore headline alone implies. Net: the commodity complex is a modest negative for AUD/CAD, roughly half the size the raw direction rules would give, and it is already embedded in the strategic Bearish on this factor rather than being a separate input.
net_commodity_exposure.scenario_oil_up_10pct: Bearish for the pair, but by less than the rules imply. Brent to roughly USD 110 lifts CAD through the energy-export channel and Australian coal and LNG partially offset on the AUD side; with Canada capturing only about three-quarters of the move after the Brent-WTI and WCS deductions, the net pair effect is a modest decline. The second-round effect cuts the other way: a higher oil price validates the RBA's permanently-higher fuel framing and the hiking option that underpins Factor 1, so the rate channel partly offsets the terms-of-trade channel.
net_commodity_exposure.scenario_oil_down_10pct: Bullish for the pair on terms of trade - Brent toward USD 90 and WTI toward the USD 83.90 Reuters consensus shrinks the Canadian surplus toward C$2-5bn and removes the Bank of Canada's own stated precondition for expecting inflation to edge up - but bearish through the Australian rate channel, since the same disinflation removes the RBA's hiking rationale. Net mildly positive for the pair, because the Canadian effect lands on both the current account and the policy rate while the Australian effect lands only on the policy rate.
net_commodity_exposure.dominant_commodity_driver: The Brent-WTI spread and the WCS differential, not the oil price itself. Whether Canada can monetise a high crude price is what separates this cross from a conventional petro-versus-metals pair, and at USD 11.05 and USD 14.80 respectively the answer is currently no. Iron ore is the second driver and is dormant pending Chinese policy in December.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: Both central banks are talking hawkish and the market believes exactly the wrong one, which is the cleanest bilateral mispricing available on this cross. The RBA's 29 September statement was unanimous, judged a further tightening in financial conditions warranted and explicitly retained the option of raising the cash rate target further if needed, with Governor Bullock describing the fuel price increase as permanently higher and naming the exchange rate as the most important transmission channel - and the market prices about 20% for 3 November. The Bank of Canada's hawkishness is louder and conditioned on a number that has already failed: Governor Macklem warned in Halifax on 21 September against responding too slowly, but tied the inflation call to oil staying near USD 100 a barrel, and WTI closed at USD 91.51 on 30 September with the Reuters 2026 consensus at USD 83.90. The 2 September deliberations are more explicit still, recording little evidence of gasoline passing through broadly and a response required only if energy spills into other CPI components - which the 1.9% trim and 2.0% median say it has not. So the market underprices guidance that is live and overprices guidance whose precondition has lapsed. The dated vehicle inside the tactical window is the Bank of Canada decision on 28 October, which the gated calendar marks as carrying the Monetary Policy Report; that is where the Bank must publish an oil assumption against its own governor's threshold.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to three months the comparison is between two credible communicators whose reaction functions point in opposite directions relative to what is priced. The RBA is the only bank in the set that has declared a supply shock permanent, which under any standard reaction function means less scope to look through an inflation overshoot - a statement about potential output, not a tactical hawkish lean. The Bank of Canada's framework is the more legible of the two, with a quarterly Monetary Policy Report cadence, a two-week Summary of Deliberations and a published neutral-rate estimate, and that legibility is precisely what makes its guidance walk-back predictable: an institution that publishes its conditions has to acknowledge when they fail. Three dated communications fall inside the horizon and the gated calendar fixes them: RBA 3 November, RBA 8 December and Bank of Canada 9 December with no projection round attached. One caution on provenance - the Australian dossier describes a quarterly Statement on Monetary Policy accompanying 3 November, but the gated calendar carries no projection-round note against that date, and where the two disagree the gated file governs, so no Australian projection round is relied on here. Confidence is 58 rather than higher because credibility cuts both ways: an RBA that has promised to hike has more to lose from stopping, and Australian unemployment at a post-COVID high makes a reversal inside the horizon a real possibility.

factors.weight_adjustment_reason: Raised +0.02 tactically and +0.01 strategically: this cross carries a genuinely one-sided, already-realised trade shock on the quote leg - US Section 338 measures escalated from a 50% duty to outright import bans on 29 September, against roughly C$20bn of Canadian retaliation - with no analogue on the base leg, where no federal election falls before 2028. Event risk is asymmetric here in a way the default weight does not capture.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The event asymmetry on this cross is the largest of any AUD pair. Canada is two days into an escalated trade conflict with the counterparty that takes 66.3% of its goods exports: Section 338 measures proclaimed on 20 July imposed a 50% ad valorem duty from 22 August and were replaced on certain products by outright import bans effective 29 September, USMCA provides no relief, the duties stack on existing AD/CVD and Section 232 measures, and Canada retaliated on 8 September with roughly C$20bn of its own. Australia has no comparable exposure - no federal election until May 2028, no new China trade restrictions identified - and its principal geopolitical exposure, the Hormuz conflict, is close to symmetric for AUD because de-escalation is risk-positive but rate-negative. For the pair, that means one leg carries a live, escalating, dated event risk and the other does not. The tactical transmission is through two Canadian prints that will carry the first measurable tariff damage: the August trade balance on 6 October, after a July print that collapsed to C$0.77bn with exports to the US down 6.6%, and the labour report on 9 October after August employment fell 41,700. The offsetting risk is real and dated: USTR has stated an end-2026 target for interim agreements, which the Canadian dossier puts at roughly 25%, and a suspension of the import bans would be the single sharpest reversal available to this cross.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Strategically the architecture matters more than any tariff line, and the architecture changed against Canada in 2026: the United States declined the sixteen-year USMCA extension at the 1 July joint review, so the agreement now runs on annual review cycles through to a 2036 expiry. Converting a settled treaty into an annually renegotiated one is a permanent increase in the risk premium on Canadian assets for an economy with two-thirds of its goods exports going to one counterparty, and it is the most plausible single explanation for why Canada's real effective exchange rate fell 1.67 points over a twelve-month period that included a record current-account surplus. Australia faces nothing structurally comparable inside the horizon; its two dated events, the China Central Economic Work Conference in December and the ongoing Hormuz negotiation, are respectively a clean AUD-positive through iron ore and a near-symmetric binary. Event clustering is worth noting and it runs in the pair's favour: Australian September-quarter CPI and the Bank of Canada's Monetary Policy Report land on the same day, 28 October, so the two legs can be repriced in the same session in the same direction. The honest counterweight, and the reason confidence is held at 58 rather than raised, is that the USTR's own end-2026 interim-deal target falls inside this horizon, and a deal is the specific way a trade-driven view on this cross is wrong quickly.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The fiscal differential between these two sovereigns is large and it is not a four-week driver. Australia holds Aaa from Moody's and AAA from S&P, Fitch and DBRS, all stable, on net general government debt of 18.8% of GDP and an underlying cash deficit of 1.6% of GDP - the strongest headline fiscal metrics in the G10. Canada holds Aaa from Moody's and AAA from S&P and DBRS but AA+ from Fitch since June 2024, on federal debt of 42.4% of GDP and a general government debt ratio of 91.8% heading to a projected 98.5% in 2027 against an AA median of 49.6%. That is a genuine gap in Australia's favour, but there is no rating review, auction event or budget inside the tactical window on either side, and neither cash curve shows a credit premium - the Government of Canada ten-year at 3.96% is orderly and the Australian ten-year trades at 5.38% on the back of a global duration selloff, not a domestic one. Transmission to a currency cross over four weeks requires an event, and there is none. Neutral at 60 reflects confidence in the conclusion rather than absence of analysis.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to three months the fiscal differential becomes a modest but real support for the pair, because the global regime is one in which sovereign balance sheets are being actively repriced - the US ten-year at the top of its one-year range and the UK ten-year the highest in the set - and in that regime relative fiscal quality discriminates. Australia has more counter-cyclical room than any economy in the benchmarking set, with net debt projected at 19.9% in 2026 rising only to 21.8% by 2028, below its own 28.3% 2020 peak; Canada is on a trajectory Fitch has publicly described as weakening its credit profile, with general government debt heading from 91.8% to a projected 98.5% of GDP and an AA+ rating from one of the four agencies already. The transmission is second-order: fiscal space lowers the probability that a policy-induced slowdown becomes disorderly, which lowers the relative risk premium on Australian assets. Confidence is only 52 for two reasons. First, Canada is actively spending that space on tariff-support programmes the Bank of Canada expects to mitigate some of the harm, which is a growth positive even as it is a ratio negative. Second, the Fitch assessment underpinning the Canadian trajectory is 322 days old and outside any reasonable freshness window, so the direction is better evidenced than the level.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to three months the only structural input remains the estimated vol surface, and at 6.798% for 190.6 days against 6.472% at 99.7 days the curve is in mild contango - the normal shape, pricing no regime change. For a cross paying 235bp of carry that matters in one specific way: a carry position is short volatility in economic substance, and a surface that prices no regime change is a surface that is not charging much for the regime change that would end the carry trade. The store's own data-quality note records that only one resistance zone met its two-touch threshold against nine support zones, which is a statement about the shape of the pair's history; this pass does not receive the zones themselves and does not use them, and a count of zones is not evidence for a fundamental stance in any case. Liquidity is the other structural fact worth stating: AUD/CAD is a second-tier cross with no listed option market, routinely traded and hedged through its two USD legs, so execution cost is effectively the sum of two legs' spreads and gap risk concentrates around sessions where both legs are repriced at once. expression_assessment.directional_expression: The vol landscape favours spot or forward over options. There is no listed option market on this cross, so an options expression means an OTC structure whose bid-offer is effectively the sum of two legs plus a correlation mark-up, and the underlying vol input is itself an estimate known to be biased low - paying a spread to own a number nobody quotes is poor practice. A spot or forward position also collects the 235bp, roughly 19 pips a month, where an option pays it away in premium. The one argument for optionality is the flat front end: four scheduled decisions inside ten weeks with no visible event kink means short-dated gamma is not being bid up for the cluster, so if an options expression is wanted the cheapest point on the curve is the near tenor. expression_assessment.event_timing_consideration: The binding cluster is 28 October, when the Bank of Canada's projection round and the Australian September-quarter CPI land in the same session - the only date in the window where both legs reprice simultaneously, which is where gap risk and slippage concentrate. The gated calendar then gives the RBA on 3 November and the pair of decisions on 8 and 9 December, so there are three further single-leg repricings inside the strategic horizon. Nothing in the term structure distinguishes any of them, which means the timing decision is a fundamental one rather than a vol-relative one.
expression_assessment.liquidity_note: AUD/CAD is a liquid minor rather than a major: it is quoted continuously but is routinely warehoused through AUD/USD and USD/CAD, so the effective spread is the sum of two legs and widens materially outside the London-New York overlap and into the Asian open. For a position whose entire carry edge is about 19 pips a month, execution cost is a first-order consideration rather than a footnote, and the two-legged structure means the pair can gap on a move in either USD leg that has nothing to do with the bilateral thesis.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: Dollar liquidity is abundant and the dollar is strong anyway, and for this cross what matters is only the differential beta of the two legs to that strength. SOFR printed 3.88% on 29 September on USD 2.967tn of volume with a 16bp percentile dispersion, reserves stand at USD 2.93tn, quantitative tightening ended in December 2025 and the balance sheet is expanding by roughly USD 17bn a month - there is no funding-stress channel operating. But the broad dollar index rose 1.884 points over the month to 120.33 at the 67th percentile of its one-year range, driven by a 2.90% ten-year real yield and a Fed that hiked unanimously on 16 September. In a US-exceptionalism dollar regime, AUD is the higher-beta leg: the Australian dossier is explicit that AUD underperforms at both ends of the dollar smile, while the Canadian dossier describes CAD as somewhat insulated from the smile's extremes by the US economic linkage. That differential beta makes a grinding dollar uptrend a modest headwind for AUD/CAD, and September bears it out in the direction of each leg against the dollar even though the cross-rate path itself is outside this pass's evidence set. Cross-currency basis for either leg could not be sourced; the -240.9bp futures roll premium against a 235bp policy differential implies the combined basis and term effect on this cross is small.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to three months the dollar headwind on this cross persists but decays. The Fed's own projections describe a committee that hikes once more and then holds through 2027 at a 4.1% median, with ample reserves and no runoff, which is a dollar that stays firm rather than one that keeps strengthening - and a flat dollar removes most of the differential-beta drag on the higher-beta leg. Both currencies have structural USD funding needs through their banking systems, Australian banks as net offshore borrowers and Canadian banks sourcing significant cross-border USD, so a basis widening would hit both rather than discriminate. The one asymmetry worth noting is the left tail: a US growth break is negative for AUD through the risk and China channels and negative for CAD through an export channel carrying 66.3% of goods exports, so neither leg is a haven and the net effect on the cross is small and uncertain. Confidence of 48 prices a genuine measurement gap - no cross-currency basis quote could be sourced for either leg at any tenor, so the funding read rests on SOFR, reserves and balance-sheet evidence rather than on basis levels.

tactical.score_interpretation: A net score of +0.3222 on a -1.00 to +1.00 scale is a clear Bullish AUD/CAD reading and, under the stated rule, derives a Bullish net stance mechanically. It is concentrated rather than broad: Policy and Rates contributes +0.1674 and Inflation and Growth +0.1044, together 84% of the gross positive, with Guidance at +0.0448 and Event Risk at +0.0406 adding the rest, against a single negative of -0.0350 from USD Liquidity. Five factors contribute exactly zero and they carry 0.34 of the tactical weight - Risk Appetite, Flows, External Balance, Fiscal and Market Structure - so a third of the book is genuinely abstaining. Breadth is not doing the work here; two rate-and-inflation factors are, and they rest on the same underlying claim that each central bank is mispriced in opposite directions.
tactical.rationale: At tactical weights this cross is decided by Policy and Rates at 0.27, Inflation and Growth at 0.18 and the two 0.07-to-0.10 factors, and three of the four point the same way. The mechanical driver is a 235bp policy differential that widened 25bp on 29 September when the RBA hiked unanimously to 4.60% while the Bank of Canada had just held at 2.25% for a seventh consecutive meeting, and the differential is backed by a 134bp ten-year gap on the payload's August monthly observations. What converts a wide differential into a tactical edge is that both legs are mispriced in the same direction: only about 20% of a 3 November RBA hike is discounted against a Board that explicitly retained the option to raise further, while the Canadian two-year at 3.37% carries 112bp above a policy rate the Bank's own operational core of 1.95% does not support. The two dossiers reinforce rather than conflict - the Australian book is tactically Bullish at +0.3040 and the Canadian book is tactically Bearish CAD at -0.2576, and a Bearish CAD standalone view is AUD/CAD-supportive by construction - so the cross expresses both views at once without the dollar leg that muddies each of them separately. The bilateral-specific modifier that neither standalone dossier captures is the capture problem in Canadian terms of trade: Brent near USD 100 reads as a CAD windfall until the USD 11.05 Brent-WTI spread and the USD 14.80 WCS discount are deducted, leaving a realised Canadian barrel near USD 76.70, which is why the quote currency's real effective exchange rate fell 1.67 points over a year in which it posted a record current-account surplus. What is priced against what we expect sits in one measurable place: the market prices the RBA as finished and the Bank of Canada as about to start, and the aggregated pair consensus of roughly 0.9898 for Q4 2026 sits marginally below spot, so a bullish view is a divergence from consensus rather than an echo of it. The path of least resistance is a carry-supported grind rather than an impulsive move, because the pair accrues roughly 19 pips a month at 235bp against an estimated 6.5-7.6% annualised volatility and the vol surface is flat across the front end. The catalyst sequence is dense and dated: Canadian trade and Ivey on 6 October, Canadian labour on 9 October, Australian labour on 15 October, Canadian CPI on 19 October, then the simultaneous Bank of Canada Monetary Policy Report and Australian September-quarter CPI on 28 October, with the RBA on 3 November immediately after the window. Conviction is 3 rather than 4 because the score is concentrated in two correlated factors, because the long is a crowded published consensus recommended by UBS, HSBC and both dossiers' own relative-value sections, and because the single largest strategic negative - a 20-point real exchange-rate gap and a 4.7pp-of-GDP current-account gap, both favouring the quote currency - is only dormant at a 0.06 tactical weight, not absent.
tactical.g10_relative_ranking: On the eleven dossiers' own tactical net scores, AUD/CAD ranks third among AUD longs: the AUD-minus-CAD spread of 0.5616 (AUD +0.3040 less CAD -0.2576) sits behind AUD/CHF at 0.5970 and a short EUR/AUD at 0.5691, and comfortably ahead of AUD/USD at 0.4862 and AUD/NZD at 0.4633. Among CAD shorts it ranks first on the same arithmetic, ahead of CAD/NOK and short EUR/CAD, because no other CAD cross pairs the quote currency against a 4.60% policy rate. The practical advantage over AUD/CHF and EUR/AUD is that AUD/CAD expresses both legs' mispricings rather than one, and the disadvantage is that both legs are commodity currencies whose terms-of-trade shocks can move together.

strategic.score_interpretation: A net score of +0.2150 derives a Bullish net stance mechanically and the reading is more broadly based than the tactical one, with five factors contributing positively and two negatively. Policy and Rates at +0.1566 and Guidance at +0.0696 are the twin engines, supported by Inflation and Growth at +0.0520, Fiscal at +0.0364 and Event Risk at +0.0348, against External Balance at -0.0960 and USD Liquidity at -0.0384. The structure of the score is the honest summary of the trade: the gross positive of +0.3494 is almost 28% consumed by a single factor, External Balance, carrying the second-heaviest weight at 0.16 and expressing a 4.7-percentage-point current-account gap and a 20-point real exchange-rate gap that both run the other way. This is a wide-carry cross with a bad valuation problem, and the score says the carry currently wins without saying it wins comfortably.
strategic.rationale: At strategic weights the book turns on Policy and Rates at 0.27, External Balance at 0.16 and Guidance at 0.12, and those three carry 55% of the weight between them with two pointing up and one pointing down hard. The rate case does not require the differential to widen, only to survive: the Bank of Canada has 50bp of room before policy becomes restrictive and an operational core of 1.95% that argues it uses none of it, while the RBA has a trimmed mean stuck at 3.6% and no comfortable route to easing, so a 235bp gap that the Canadian curve prices to compress by roughly 50bp is more likely to hold near 210-235bp. Guidance reinforces this through a specific and testable asymmetry - the RBA's retained hiking option is priced at about a fifth of its stated probability, while the Bank of Canada's hawkish framing was conditioned on oil near USD 100 and WTI closed at USD 91.51 with the Reuters 2026 consensus at USD 83.90 - and the two errors resolve in the same direction for this cross. The standalone dossiers interact in the pair's favour at this horizon more than at the tactical one: the Australian book is strategically Neutral at +0.0307 while the Canadian book is strategically Bearish CAD at -0.3646 and ranks CAD last of eleven, so the AUD-minus-CAD spread of 0.3953 is the widest of any AUD cross. The bilateral factors that modify the standalone views are the Canadian trade architecture and the Canadian oil capture problem: Section 338 import bans took effect on 29 September inside a USMCA that the United States declined to extend for sixteen years and that now runs on annual review through 2036, and the realised Canadian barrel near USD 76.70 against a USD 100 Brent headline means the energy windfall does not reach the currency. Against all of that sits the one factor that genuinely frightens this trade: Australia's real effective exchange rate at 116.11 is the highest in the benchmarking set and up 9.97% in a year in which iron ore fell 7.14%, while Canada's at 96.29 is the second cheapest, and Australia runs a 3.67%-of-GDP current-account deficit against Canada's 1.03% surplus. That is a stock imbalance of the kind that resolves through the exchange rate over quarters, and it is why the strategic conviction is 2 while the score is +0.2150. What is priced is captured by the aggregated pair consensus, which sits at roughly 0.9898 for Q4 2026 and 0.9850 by mid-2027 with a bearish provider bias - a market expecting the carry to be slowly given back - against UBS and HSBC, who publish the long. The path of least resistance is a carry-accruing grind rather than a trend, with the dated decision points being the Bank of Canada Monetary Policy Report on 28 October, the RBA on 3 November, the RBA on 8 December and the Bank of Canada on 9 December, plus the USTR's end-2026 target for USMCA interim agreements, which is the single catalyst capable of reversing the Event Risk and External Balance factors together.

Among CAD shorts it also ranks first by score, though CAD/NOK is the cleaner relative-value expression of the petro-currency thesis specifically, since Norway captures the Brent premium Canada cannot and pays 225bp of carry while doing it. The ranking caveat is that AUD/CAD gets its top place from the weakness of the quote leg rather than the strength of the base leg, which is a different and slightly less durable thing.

consensus_divergence.our_strategic_view: Bullish AUD/CAD, conviction 2, net weighted score +0.2150. The pair rises over one to three months on carry and relative policy, against a real and quantified valuation and external-balance headwind that caps conviction at 2 rather than 3.
consensus_divergence.divergence_direction: Above consensus on both horizons. The four-provider aggregate has the pair marginally below spot at Q4 2026 and declining through 2027; we expect it higher. We sit with UBS and HSBC and against the aggregate and against RBC's carry-sputtering framing.
consensus_divergence.divergence_magnitude: Pass 2 level comparison against the aggregate path: about +84 pips at ~1 month (our probability-weighted 0.9975 vs 0.98908), about +169 pips at ~6 months (1.0005 vs 0.98362), and +214 pips at end-March 2027 on the base case (1.0050 vs 0.98362). Pass 1 was directional only: the aggregate Q4 2026 figure of roughly 0.9898 sits a little below the 0.99123 spot and the mid-2027 figure of 0.9850 further below, so our Bullish stance diverges on direction and widens with tenor; UBS, the one bank with a published pair target, is above spot and on our side.
consensus_divergence.why_we_differ: Three things the aggregate underweights. First, the symmetry of the two mispricings: consensus treats the RBA as finished and the Bank of Canada as about to start, when the Australian trimmed mean is 3.6% and the Canadian trim-median average is 1.95% - the Canadian curve carries 112bp of hike premium in the two-year that the Bank's own core measure cannot justify, while the RBA's retained hiking option is priced at about a fifth of its stated probability. Second, the oil capture problem: forecasts that treat Brent near USD 100 as a Canadian terms-of-trade windfall are using the wrong barrel, because the Brent-WTI spread is USD 11.05 against USD 4.08 a year earlier and WCS settles USD 14.80 under WTI, leaving a realised Canadian barrel near USD 76.70 - a 23% haircut that is a pipeline-capacity tax no price move removes. Third, the permanence of the trade shock: Section 338 measures escalated from duty to outright import ban on 29 September inside a USMCA the United States refused to extend for sixteen years, and no published forecast embeds an annually renegotiated treaty as a standing risk premium on Canadian assets. Where we agree with consensus is on the valuation problem: a 116.11 Australian real effective exchange rate against 96.29 for Canada is exactly why the aggregate is bearish over 2027, and it is why our strategic conviction is 2. We are above the aggregate because it extrapolates a slow return of carry; we expect the 28 October cluster to confirm that the Bank of Canada is overpriced.
consensus_divergence.payoff_if_right: The carry does part of the work regardless of direction - roughly 19 pips a month at 235bp, the best risk-adjusted carry on any AUD cross bar AUD/CHF at an estimated 0.31-0.36 carry-to-vol. Beyond that, being right means the pair rises against an aggregate consensus that has it falling, and the relative-value payoff is larger than the outright one because the same view expressed against the dollar on either leg is diluted by a dollar that is strong for reasons unrelated to either currency.
consensus_divergence.risk_if_wrong: The specific way this is wrong is a USTR-Canada interim agreement inside the stated end-2026 window that suspends the Section 338 import bans, which would reverse Event Risk and relieve External Balance simultaneously - the Canadian dossier puts it near 25%. The slower way is the valuation channel: a 20-point real exchange-rate gap and a 4.7pp-of-GDP current-account gap resolving through the exchange rate, with a crowded published consensus long on the other side of it. A Hormuz escalation that pushes WTI above USD 100 while the Brent-WTI spread narrows would restore both the Bank of Canada's stated precondition and Canada's revenue capture at once, which is the cleanest single-event reversal available. If wrong, the published aggregate path costs roughly 100–200 pips against a position that has accrued roughly 60–116 pips of carry over three to six months.

cross_horizon_consistency.explanation: Both horizons are Bullish and the direction is the same, but the composition changes materially and the score decays by about a third. Tactically the case is concentrated: Policy and Rates plus Inflation and Growth supply 84% of the gross positive, five factors abstain, and External Balance is dormant at a 0.06 weight. Strategically the case broadens - Guidance rises to 0.12, Fiscal turns positive and Event Risk persists - but External Balance rises from 0.06 to 0.16 and turns Bearish, consuming 28% of the gross positive on its own. Nothing about either currency changes between the horizons; what changes is whether a 235bp carry differential or a 20-point real exchange-rate gap is being weighted, and the strategic book weights the second one heavily enough to cut conviction from 3 to 2 without flipping the sign.
cross_horizon_consistency.trading_implication: The direction does not need to be re-established across the transition, but the sizing does. The tactical window has two datable pricing errors with a dated resolution in the 28 October cluster and the 3 November RBA decision; the strategic window has the same carry running against a valuation and external-balance imbalance that compounds with time. The honest reading is a position whose justification is strongest in the first four to six weeks and whose risk profile deteriorates as the horizon lengthens, which argues for treating the strategic Bullish as a carry-and-policy hold to be reviewed at the December decisions rather than as a conviction trend view. The two conditions that would convert strategic conviction 2 into 3 are a USTR interim-deal deadline passing without an agreement and the Australian real effective exchange rate retreating below 110 while the differential holds; the conditions that would cut it to 1 are a Bank of Canada hike with forward guidance attached, or an RBA communication that removes the hiking option. Pass-2 price note: the price structure supports a single position with two sizing tiers - the tactical tier risk-budgeted to the 0.9795 daily-close stop and reviewed at 3 November, and the strategic residual held at half that risk to the 0.9680 weekly-close stop and reviewed at the 8–9 December decisions.

catalysts.event: Canada merchandise trade balance (August), exports and imports, plus September Ivey PMI
catalysts.rationale: The first print that can carry a full month of the 50% Section 338 duty regime, ahead of the import bans that took effect 29 September. July collapsed to +C$0.77bn from +C$4.2bn with exports to the United States down 6.6%, so this is the direct test of whether the record Q2 current-account surplus - the single strongest fundamental argument against this pair - is already reversing. A further narrowing weakens the quote leg's external case while the base leg's is unchanged.

catalysts.event: Canada Labour Force Survey (September), released alongside US non-farm payrolls
catalysts.rationale: August employment fell 41,700 with full-time down 35,900 and permanent-employee wage growth halved to 2.0%, against unemployment already at 6.4% versus Australia's 4.6%. A second negative print removes the labour-market support for the roughly 120bp of Bank of Canada tightening in the curve and pushes the 112bp of premium out of the Canadian two-year, widening the expected differential in the pair's favour without requiring anything from the RBA.

Australian unemployment reached a post-COVID high of 4.6% in August with the entire 39,000 employment gain in part-time work. A third consecutive rise starts the market pricing an RBA pivot and undermines Factor 1 and Factor 6 together, which carry 0.34 of the tactical weight on this cross; a fall back to 4.5% with full-time gains removes the main obstacle to a 3 November hike. The surprise is genuinely two-sided for the base leg.

Headline held at 3.0% in August purely on gasoline at plus 22.8% year on year while CPI-trim printed 1.9% and CPI-median 2.0%. As the fuel base effect rolls off with WTI at USD 91.51 and a 2026 consensus of USD 83.90, headline converges toward the 2.4% ex-gasoline rate, which is a downside surprise against hike pricing and widens the core inflation gap against Australia's 3.6% trimmed mean.

catalysts.event: Bank of Canada decision with Monetary Policy Report (the only projection round in the gated calendar inside this window)
catalysts.rationale: The highest-leverage single date for this cross. The Bank must publish an oil assumption against Governor Macklem's own statement that inflation would edge up if oil stayed near USD 100, with WTI at USD 91.51, and it does so with a Canadian two-year carrying 112bp above a 2.25% policy rate that an operational core of 1.95% does not support. A hold that lowers the oil assumption bleeds premium out of the quote leg's front end and widens the expected policy differential.

catalysts.event: ABS Consumer Price Index, September quarter 2026 (same session as the Bank of Canada projection round)
catalysts.rationale: The highest-impact Australian release in the window, and it clusters with the Canadian decision so both legs can reprice in a single session. The monthly indicator has already re-accelerated to 4.0% while trimmed mean has held at 3.6% for three months; a trimmed mean at or above 3.7% moves 3 November hike pricing from about 20% through 50%. Event clustering amplifies rather than cancels here, because the plausible surprises on the two legs point the same way for the pair.

catalysts.event: Reserve Bank of Australia Monetary Policy Board decision (gated calendar; no projection-round note attached)
catalysts.rationale: The resolution point for the base leg's tactical thesis, five days after Australian Q3 CPI. The Board hiked unanimously on 29 September and explicitly retained the option of raising further, yet about 20% and roughly 7bp of a 25bp step are discounted. Delivery widens the differential to 260bp; a hold that keeps the option alive leaves it at 235bp. Note that the gated calendar attaches no projection-round flag to this date, so the Australian dossier's description of an accompanying Statement on Monetary Policy is not relied upon.

catalysts.event: ABS Wage Price Index, September quarter 2026
catalysts.rationale: Australian wage growth of 3.2% year on year sits below headline CPI, so real wages have fallen for three consecutive quarters, which is the evidence that the inflation shock is cost-push rather than wage-driven. A further deceleration strengthens the case that the RBA can stop, removing the base leg's rate support at the margin and narrowing the only differential this cross genuinely trades on.

On the trajectory from 4.5% in July to 4.6% in August, this is the release that determines whether 5.0% Australian unemployment arrives inside the strategic window. A print at 4.8% or above begins the pivot repricing that would compress the differential from the base side, which is the main domestic route by which the strategic Bullish becomes wrong without anything changing in Canada.

catalysts.event: Canada Q3 2026 GDP and monthly GDP for September (Statistics Canada end-of-month cadence; not confirmed in the gated calendar)
catalysts.rationale: Q2 grew 3.3% annualised but monthly tracking has stalled at 0.0% then 0.2%, and this is the first full quarter under the Section 338 duty regime. Macklem's own tariff-conditional estimate for Q4 is below 1%. A weak print widens the growth differential against Australia's 2.14% year on year and removes the resilience argument that underpins the constructive sell-side case on the quote leg.

catalysts.event: Reserve Bank of Australia Monetary Policy Board decision (gated calendar)
catalysts.rationale: The last Australian decision of 2026 and the one that settles whether the cycle peaked at 4.60% or extends. If November delivered, this is the hold that defines the peak; if November held, this becomes the live meeting with October and November data in hand. The two outcomes bracket the base leg's contribution to the differential for the remainder of the strategic horizon.

catalysts.event: Bank of Canada decision (gated calendar; no projection round attached)
catalysts.rationale: Falling one day after the RBA, this is the sequencing that matters most inside the strategic horizon: the Australian decision sets the tone and the Canadian one either validates or refutes the roughly two hikes by January that the Canadian curve carries. A second consecutive hold after an October Monetary Policy Report that lowered the oil assumption makes that pricing untenable and is the most likely point at which the 112bp of Canadian two-year premium is given back.

catalysts.event: China Central Economic Work Conference (week-dated; sets the 2027 growth target and stimulus envelope)
catalysts.rationale: The one strategic event with a clean base-leg-positive sign. China takes 30-35% of Australian exports and the transmission is iron ore, which at USD 96.59 and down 7.14% over twelve months prices no stimulus impulse. A property or infrastructure package would restore the terms-of-trade support that the base leg's real exchange rate currently lacks and would partially neutralise the External Balance factor that is the largest strategic negative on this cross.

catalysts.event: USTR target date for USMCA interim agreements
catalysts.rationale: The single largest reversal risk to this pair's thesis and the one catalyst that would move the Event Risk and External Balance factors together. An interim deal that suspends the 29 September Section 338 import bans removes a standing risk premium on Canadian assets that is the most plausible explanation for the quote currency's real exchange rate falling 1.67 points through a record current-account surplus. Failure entrenches that premium inside a treaty now on annual review through 2036.

assumptions: Price series as delivered (payload metadata): dataPoints 130; dateRange 2026-04-06 to 2026-10-02; spot 0.99123; spotDate 2026-10-02; computationRange 2007-12-24 to 2026-10-02 (4900 weekday bars). Data quality lines: 'AUD/CAD: only 1 resistance / 9 support zones met the 2-touch threshold — supplement with round numbers and note the shortfall'; 'AUD/CAD: 4900 weekday bars in the store (2007-12-24 to 2026-10-02); 1007 weekly, 500 monthly; 130 daily bars passed downstream (2026-04-06 to 2026-10-02), which is the 1-6 month strategic horizon'.

Spot date gap: spotDate (2026-10-02) is one trading session after the 2026-10-01 valuation date. Every level, pip distance, percentage and forward in the report is anchored to 0.99123. No web quote was substituted.

Moving averages are simple averages of trading-day closes over the full stored history; the 200-week average and its +0.000562-per-week slope are taken directly from the payload. Realised volatility is annualised on 252 days. Range percentile is quoted on the closing basis (90), which equals the intraday basis (90). Pip distances to zones are measured to the zone midpoint, as the store computes them.

Resistance shortfall: only one computed resistance zone qualified. The ladder above it (parity/1.00137, 1.0100, 1.0200) is round-number and observed-extreme supplementation and is weaker evidence than the touch-counted zone.

Implied volatility is the store's triangle estimate (realised correlation 0.5608), cited as an estimate and treated as a floor, with a 7.0–7.6% working range where the documented understatement matters. No IV percentile, risk reversal, barrier or vol-surface quote exists for AUD/CAD in any free source; the schema fields iv_percentile and CFTC percentiles are therefore null because the report does not supply them.

Forward outrights are derived from the -240.9bp futures roll premium, applied linearly on simple interest over 30, 91 and 182 days. The roll bundles the rate differential with the cross-currency basis, and the two cannot be separated without an OIS curve.

The 10-year yields in the rates block are MONTHLY observations as of 2026-08-01 and are not quoted as live levels. The +161bp two-year spread combines the AUD dossier's 2026-09-30 Australian 2Y (4.98%) with the CAD dossier's 2026-09-28 Canadian 2Y (3.37%); the dates differ by two days.

Scenario probabilities are the analyst's own and sum to 100% on each horizon. Expected values are probability-weighted pips from spot; carry is reported separately rather than added in. Sizing guidance is a risk-budget illustration (0.50% of capital tactically, 0.25% strategically, to the stated stops), not a trade structure.

Weights, factors and synthesis are carried verbatim from the pass-1 Direction Verdict. Factor 9's verbatim text describes the chart as withheld, which was true for pass 1; the pass-2 technical supplement is additive and does not change the scored stance. In the weight_adjustments array the numeric default and applied weights are the tactical values; strategic values are stated in each reason.

Disclosed reservation: since pass 1 scored, a report on 5 October described moderating Australian domestic price pressures, which cuts against the tactical Factor 2 and Factor 6 thesis on the base leg. The chart also shows a clean rejection at parity, and the refreshed aggregate consensus sits below spot. The verdict stands as issued; these points are reflected in the levels (parity treated as resistance until a close above 1.00137), the dip-entry construction and the downside scenario, not in any re-scoring.

Research scope: bilateral web research covered pair forecasts, chart commentary and fresh leg-specific news. Extrapolation-model forecast sites (TradersUnion, PandaForecast, CoinCodex, 30rates, AUDToday) were returned by search and excluded as a category error. Bilateral trade comes from the injected IMF DOTS block, not re-estimated.
